title: Nepotism: When Hiring the Best Just Won't Do
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore nepotism: its definition, the workplace and family-business risks, the biological sense (kin selection and Hamilton's rule), the word's origin in the Latin "nepos" (nephew) and Catholic priests, the three types (self-determined, coercive, opportunistic) illustrated by The Godfather characters, and its role in government, including U.S. White House staffing rules and the Kennedy and Trump-era examples. They also discuss meritocracy versus nepotism, monarchy and primogeniture, discrimination and sexism in anti-nepotism rules, legacy admissions, and a study linking family-based CEO promotions to weaker performance. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about private ambulances and a brief sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and McDonald's
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about McDonald's menu items (Big Mac, Quarter Pounder, double cheeseburger, McDLT) before moving to the topic.

segments.title: Nepotism in family businesses
segments.summary: Using a franchise-passing-to-daughter example, the hosts explain that handing a family business to relatives is nepotism, with experts advising outside experience first, and the morale and fairness problems this creates for other employees. They note the 'third generation ruins the business' saying.

segments.title: Nepotism in nature and kin selection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Grabst article's view that nepotism underlies civilization and the tension with meritocracy, and the biological sense of nepotism, with squirrel warning calls as an example of kin selection.

segments.title: Hamilton's rule
segments.summary: Hamilton's rule is explained as rB > C, relating genetic relatedness, benefit, and cost, illustrated with worker bees and the queen. Chuck calls the formula reductive.

segments.title: Etymology of nepotism
segments.summary: The word comes from Latin nepos, meaning nephew, reportedly because Catholic priests called their illegitimate children nephews. Adam Bellow's Atlantic article is mentioned.

segments.title: Three types of nepotism
segments.summary: The hosts describe the three types from the Grabst article (self-determined, coercive, opportunistic), matching them to Godfather characters Sonny, Michael, and Fredo.

segments.title: Nepotism vs cronyism and government nepotism
segments.summary: Definitions of nepotism and cronyism. Discussion of healthy mix of merit and family ties, and of government as the sector where nepotism is most frowned upon, with the Kennedy appointment of Bobby as attorney general and the later rule changes on White House staff family members, including the 2017 DOJ ruling.

segments.title: Nepotism and democracy and Kushner
segments.summary: The hosts argue nepotism harms checks and balances and loyalty to institutions, and discuss Jared Kushner's White House role and his loyalty-to-family remark.

segments.title: Family as basic unit and cults
segments.summary: The hosts describe the family as the basic unit of society and note that cults break apart families. They briefly discuss the Netflix documentary Wild Wild Country and Black Mirror.

segments.title: Confucianism, Roman Empire, monarchy, and primogeniture
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Confucian views on family loyalty, the swing between meritocracy and nepotism, the Roman Empire's decline from promoting relatives, primogeniture and monarchy, and the American founding's rejection of inherited titles and estates, with Thomas Jefferson.

segments.title: Discrimination, dream hoarders, and legacy admissions
segments.summary: Nepotism is described as a form of discrimination by class and race and as sexist when anti-nepotism laws were no-spouse rules. Positive nepotism is considered via Spike Lee's hiring. A study finds a medical school admission advantage for children of doctors, and a study finds family-based CEO promotions perform 14 percent worse. The Boston Review's 'Dream Hoarders' article is cited.

segments.title: Family-business succession advice and goat banking
segments.summary: The hosts conclude that a planned, outside-experience path works better for family successors, especially in idiosyncratic businesses, with jokes about goat banking and cobbling.

segments.title: Listener mail: private ambulances
segments.summary: Listener Jay Haley, who has nearly twenty years of EMS experience, explains for-profit and nonprofit private ambulances and their contracts with hospitals, nursing homes, and municipalities. The hosts also share a story about a cab driver who took a passenger to hospice.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for listener stories and provide social media and website contact information.
